title: How a small Army team built a lightweight battle planning app: Odin - Breaking Defense
html:
FORT BELVOIR, Va. — A team at the Army’s C5ISR Center on Fort Belvoir, Va., is working on a project dubbed Odin, which could be the service’s new AI-enhanced mission planning app for tactical units.

“We found that there was a gap in the Army at the tactical level,” Maj. Andrew Durfee, who heads the Odin team, said in a interview with Breaking Defense. “There’s robust mission planning capabilities at the division and the corps levels, [but] the farther that you get to that forward line of troops — what a lot of people reference as the ‘tactical edge’ — you have minimized compute, you have minimized bandwidth.”

Software optimized for brigades and above, where large staffs have bulky generators to power an arsenal of laptops, routers and servers, doesn’t necessarily translate to battalion and below, where a handful of officers and non-commissioned officers have to sketch out plans using militarized tablets and smartphones, he explained.

“Odin was created to basically bridge that gap … at the battalion, company and platoon level,” Durfee said.

Odin is now being integrated into the Army’s official battle network program, Next Generation Command and Control (NGC2), under a kind of “app store” or “ecosystem” approach to incorporating innovative software tools from non-traditional sources.

“We’ve done a tremendous amount of work with both Palantir and Anduril,” Durfee said, particularly on smoothly sharing data. Earlier versions of the software were field-tested by the 4th Infantry Division and other units, including at this summer’s Project Convergence Capstone 6 (PCC-6) exercise, providing both positive feedback and critique to drive improvements.

“Over the last year we have had significant increase in capabilities,” Durfee said. Next year, the team aims to test the latest upgrades at PCC-7, roll out an official Minimum Viable Capability Release, and then hand over a mature version of Odin to the Army’s portfolio acquisition executive (PAE) for command and control systems.

While the developers keep adding features, Odin at its core is a way to automate planning processes traditionally done on paper — or, in some cases, Durfee recalls, drawn on the back of a used MRE ration box.

As a young officer, Durfee said, he often found himself “frantically writing down notes” while his superiors outlined a complex plan over the radio. Other times he’d wait for a courier from higher headquarters to arrive with a print-out or even hand-drawn diagrams of where to maneuver.

Odin allows frontline troops to exchange those detailed orders and map graphics electronically. It also taps into larger Army command networks — that’s where the collaboration with Anduril and Palantir comes in — to pull down data and automatically update the situation maps accordingly. That allows commanders to answer pressing tactical questions at a glance, instead of trying to make multiple radio calls and pull the details together in their head.

“Where is the enemy? Where are my friendly forces?” Durfee said. “What does the weather look like? Where are my sensors? What is the [intelligence] collection plan looking like?”

Odin can even help users visualize the “fog of war” by showing them the regions on the map where no friendly unit can see — either because it’s too far or blocked by an obstacle — which highlights gaps in their awareness where enemies might lurk unseen.

“We’ve seen this be very effective at PCC-6,” Durfee said, where one unit used the fog-of-war map to figure out which routes risked an ambush and which were safe to take. Now the team is working to add similar “where we can see/where we can’t” mapping for infrared sensors, radar and radio transmissions.

The team’s biggest ambition is to build what they call a “course of action generator,” using AI to help suggest everything from safe routes to entire schemes of maneuver. That goal’s beyond what the Fort Belvoir team can do itself, Durfee acknowledges, and it’ll be a challenge to get such complex software — which other military branches have experimented with — to run on the modest hardware a junior officer can carry into combat.

“We’re doing a heavy involvement with industry because … [these capabilities] require a robust amount of processing, compute power,” Durfee said. For now, he said, “we’re building a very light version.”
summary: Software optimized for brigades and above, where large staffs have bulky generators to power an arsenal of laptops, routers, and servers, doesn’t necessarily translate to battalion and below, Maj. Andrew Durfee explained to Breaking Defense.
